query: For high-entropy alloys intended for extreme environments, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties? State the intervention without limiting its class, the proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the temperature and application boundaries under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose outcome would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A slower cooling rate during the solution heat treatment of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) induces serrated grain boundary morphology, which in turn improves elevated-temperature mechanical properties by reducing local strain concentrations and impeding intergranular crack propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory or high-temperature HEA produced by standard processing routes (e.g., via selective laser melting or conventional casting) that exhibits predominantly straight grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a modified heat treatment with a controlled, slower cooling rate during solution treatment to promote the formation of serrated (undulated) grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Tested at elevated temperatures appropriate for extreme environment applications such as those in nuclear reactors or aerospace systems.
generation.structural_mediator: Serrated grain boundaries, characterized by an undulated morphology with increased relative wave features compared to straight boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The serrated grain boundaries distribute local strains more evenly, reducing strain concentration at triple junctions and deflecting or delaying intergranular crack propagation, thereby enhancing both ductility and creep resistance at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to HEAs with straight grain boundaries, the intervention is predicted to increase the tensile fracture strain by around a factor of 3.5 and reduce the minimum creep strain rate by roughly 96% at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: HEA samples processed under conventional rapid cooling conditions that result in straight grain boundaries and exhibit relatively lower high-temperature ductility and higher creep strain rates.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected primarily in HEAs used for extreme high-temperature applications (e.g., 650°C to 982°C) and may depend on both the alloy composition and the specifics of the processing method (such as in additively manufactured components).
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement may vary with the exact alloy system, heat treatment parameters, and measurement conditions. Further systematic experiments are required to optimize the cooling rate for specific HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples with identical compositions. One set undergoes standard rapid cooling solution heat treatment (yielding predominantly straight grain boundaries), while the other set undergoes a controlled, slower cooling rate during solution treatment designed to induce serrated grain boundaries. Characterize the grain boundary morphology using microscopy techniques and then perform tensile and creep tests at elevated temperatures (e.g., at 650°C and 982°C).
measurements: Grain boundary morphology (quantitative measures of serration amplitude and wavelength)
Tensile fracture strain and yield strength at elevated temperatures
Minimum creep strain rates and creep rupture life
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slowed-cooling treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in elevated-temperature ductility (i.e., higher tensile fracture strain) and demonstrate reduced creep strain rates and extended creep life compared to the rapidly cooled baseline samples, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. However, thermo-mechanical process is not applicable as a post processing step for SLM, where components are usually built closely to the final dimension. Another possible approach to resolve the hot ductility loss is to introduce serrated grain boundary (SEGB) [], it usually involves a post heat treatment step to induce interactions between mobile grain boundaries and second phases, including carbides [], δ phase [], or γ′ phase []. SEGB has been reported to impede intergranular crack propagation [,,], improve the tensile properties of Ni-based superalloys fabricated by SLM [], and also the ductility of Ni46.23Co23Cr10Fe5Al8.5Ti4W2Mo1C0.15B0.1Zr0.02 fabricated by arc melting []. In this study, we have unprecedentedly utilized SEGB on an HEA fabricated by SLM. This work is the first to investigate the underlying mechanism of hot ductility drop of a HEA fabricated by SLM and study the effect of SEGB on its high temperature tensile and creep properties.
